brief_definition.zh: 一种利用“可见性”的不对称，将外部权力内化为自我规训的控制机制
brief_definition.en: A control mechanism that exploits the "asymmetry of visibility" to compel self-discipline.

zh: 想象一座环形的建筑，中心矗立着一座瞭望塔，四周环绕着一间间独立的囚室。由于特殊的照明设计（逆光），处于中心塔楼的狱警可以随时看到任何一间囚室，但囚室中的犯人却无法看到塔楼里是否有人。 这种结构被称为“全景敞视监狱”（Panopticon）。该词由英国哲学家杰里米·边沁（Jeremy Bentham）于1791年提出，由前缀 "Pan-"（全部）和词根 "-opticon"（视觉）组成，意为“全知全视”。边沁认为这是一种廉价且高效的管理方案：因为囚徒无法确认自己何时被查看，为了避免惩罚，他们必须假设自己时刻处于监视之下。

约200年后，法国哲学家米歇尔·福柯（Michel Foucault）在《规训与惩罚》中重新审视了这一提案。他指出，“全景敞视”不应仅被视为一种建筑设计，更是一种精密控制的抽象概念和现代社会的权力图示（Diagram of Power）。 这种机制早已溢出了监狱的高墙，被广泛应用于工厂、学校、医院和办公室。在这些场所中，权力不再需要通过肉体的酷刑来展示，而是通过无所不在的规则和潜在的目光，迫使个体产生心理上的自我约束。今天的学术讨论沿用了福柯的文本意义，指涉现代人被权力所控制、被规则所操纵的普遍境地。
en: Imagine a circular prison with a watchtower at its center, surrounded by individual cells. Due to backlighting, the inmates cannot discern if they are being watched by the warden in the central tower.

This structure is known as the "Panopticon." Proposed by English philosopher Jeremy Bentham in 1791, the term combines the prefix "Pan-" (all) and the root "-opticon" (visual), literally meaning "all-seeing." Bentham conceived of this as a cost-effective and efficient management solution: since inmates can never know for sure whether they are being watched, they must assume they are under constant surveillance to avoid punishment.

Approximately 200 years later, French philosopher Michel Foucault re-examined this proposal in Discipline and Punish. He argued that the Panopticon should not be viewed merely as an architectural design, but as an abstract concept of precise control and a diagram of power for modern society.

This mechanism has long since extended beyond prison walls, finding wide application in factories, schools, hospitals, and offices. In these settings, power is no longer exercised through physical torture but through ubiquitous rules and the potential gaze, compelling individuals into self-discipline. Current academic discourse adopts Foucault’s interpretation, referring to the condition of modern individuals controlled by power and manipulated by rules.

example_sentence.zh: 随着无处不在的摄像头和大数据算法的普及，现代都市正在演变成一座巨大的数字化全景敞视监狱，我们即便身处家中，也时刻处于一种被观看的焦虑之中。
example_sentence.en: With the proliferation of ubiquitous surveillance cameras and big data algorithms, the modern city is evolving into a vast digital Panopticon. Even when at home, we remain constantly gripped by the anxiety of being watched.

content.zh: 当权力所需要的舞台从实体建筑转向了虚拟的互联世界，具体的管教场所还是否沿用圆形监狱的形式就不再重要了。因为权力的所有方早已有更轻盈、更无形却也更具渗透性的意识形态武器来完成从前只有砖混巨物才能达成的成效。
content.en: When the stage of power shifts from physical buildings to the virtual world, the specific form of the disciplinary site becomes less important. Those in power have lighter, invisible, yet more pervasive ideological weapons to achieve what once required a masonry colossus.

content.zh:
全景敞视监狱也被译作圆形监狱。作为建筑学中最广为流行的几个概念之一，我们在对它的解释中主要想指出这样两个问题。这篇文章于2020年6月发布在沙丘研究所的公众号上——

第一，“全景敞视主义”不止是被监视情况下的规训，它也是对于群体流动性的压制。

第二，“圆形监狱”虽然作为一个空间样板或者社会比喻无比成功，但作为实际建成项目，这些监狱的价值显得相对平庸。

以下是原文：

怎样把一群野蛮人变成现代人？

步骤一，把他们放在一个个小格间里；
步骤二，让他们知道自己的行为一直被监视着；
步骤三，把他们隔离起来，保证他们无法成群结队。

上述的这种改造或教化的过程，可以作为米歇尔·福柯《规训与惩罚》中“全景敞视主义”的简化概括。

1. 作为诊断书或说明书

作为一个非传统的思考者，福柯的写作“易于感觉但难于确定”。这种权力技术——或空间样板——似乎既是一份说明书也是一份诊断书。它作为说明书的意义，回应的也就是文章开头的那个问题：怎么把一群骚动、野蛮、冲动的“乌合之众”转化成有秩序、可管理、拥有生产力的现代人？而作为一份诊断书，它回应了这样一个问题：既然现代社会看起来如此井然有序、亮丽美好，那么，为什么其中这么多人感到无比焦虑和抑郁？

如果回到这项概念被提出的原始文本，不难发现杰里米·边沁最初在1787年写成的文章《圆形监狱（#Panopticon: or the Inspection House#）》显然是作为一份说明书出现的——那是一项提案，一次设计，一份乌托邦式的畅想（严格意义上说，杰里米·边沁的弟弟萨缪尔·边沁是“圆形监狱”的首次提出者，他观察到了俄罗斯工厂当中的“中心视察原则（central inspection principle）”。后来杰里米·边沁化用了这项原则到他的监狱提案中。）；而福柯在约200年后写成的《规训与惩罚》则是作为一份诊断书的姿态面世。尤在《全景敞视主义》那一章中，法国学者重新挖掘了那位英国法理学家所设想的监狱方案，并且一针见血地指出，边沁提出的“改造所”，当它不是作为严格意义上的建成项目，而是作为一种抽象的模式，已经成为了当时西方现代社会的压倒性状况——远不只是监狱，“全景敞视模式”已被广泛用在了精神病院、工厂、学校、办公室当中……所以在1970年代，由福柯的重新介绍，“圆形监狱”作为一种话语，更多时候成为了令人不寒而栗的、反乌托邦式的社会批评。今天的建筑学范畴或者更广泛的学术界沿用了福柯的文本意义。我们使用这个概念的时候，基本把它作为“白色恐怖”和“精神奴役”的代名词，指涉现代人被威权所控制、被规则所操纵的不幸境地。

2. “圆形监狱”消解了聚集场面

这个广负盛名的学术概念因高度准确地描述了社会现状，而越来越频繁地走入大众的、公共的讨论当中。但需要注意的是，今天大量文章对于“全景敞视主义”的解读，似乎很多时候存在一定的偏狭——人们更多着迷于这项空间样板中“老大哥在看着你”的部分，也就是我们开头简化场景中的第二步。

可以理解，“panopticon”一词的词根“pan- (all，全）”和“optic (seeing，看)”组合在一起的本意即是“all-seeing，一览无余”，这其实和另一个词“omniscient，全知全能”在组成上十分相似（后者同样是由“omni-，全”和“scire，知晓”）。

所以，词汇本身即着重强调了位处中心的瞭望塔的地位。因而，对于这项概念，许多讨论也都详述了个体无时无刻不被凝视，行为不敢越轨，以至于到最后即便管理者已经缺席，个体还是会持续地进行“自我凝视”和“自我管理”的情况。在当下的世界，或许正是因为密集的监控系统和普遍的审查机制，写作者也就主要运用圆形监狱中这项“看与被看”的经典关系对现实进行诠释。

不过这并不是“全景敞视主义”的全部。

“他的房间被安排成正对着中心瞭望塔，这就使他有一种向心的可见性。但是环形建筑被分割成囚室，则意味着一种横向的不可见性。”

另一项同等、甚至更加重要的要素是开头简化场景中的第三步：在圆形监狱当中，每一个个体都陷入了绝对隔离的孤立境地当中，他们相互之间不能够顺畅交流，不能够抱团，不能够凝聚在一起成为所谓“群体”。所以，这项权力技术将保证这些个体总是等级制度中被动的一方，并永远无法调转这项关系；从交往理论的眼光看来，它使得“讨论”消亡了，也消解了公共领域产生的可能性。

为什么一定要把人打散？为什么一定要防止他们聚集在一起形成公众？此时我们不妨重新回到边沁的时代。18世纪末，这位法理学家正为自己提出的这项优秀方案心潮澎湃，以至于带着它四处奔走推销。他不是一个“疯狂的邪恶科学家”，他的这项空间的构想显然也不是出于纯然“恶”的意图。相反，边沁把它当做一个良性的“改造所”。他设想，在这个地方，病态的、偏离的、有罪的人和念头，将被秩序、理性和道德的观念改造，这将是一个带我们走向文明的催化所。

人民串联、聚集在一起的场面总会令当权者警惕，因为相比于零散的个体，群体是“有力量的”。我们同样需要明白的一点是，并不是个体聚集在一起所形成的的“群众”都会是高尚、道德、追随至高信仰、甘于牺牲自我的“伟大的群众”。当个体来到一起，一份独立的“群体精神”似乎就在驾驭其中的个体，以至于释放出个体在平常近乎被压抑着的，某种蠢动的动物性能量。

“群众的民主权力就像一切个人权力一样，当它没有受到恰当的宪政约束时，也很容易转变为它的反面，成为一种暴虐的权力。”此时“思想和感觉中道德约束与文明方式突然消失，原始冲动、幼稚行为和犯罪倾向突然爆发”。换句话说，当个体聚集在一起形成群众之后，每一个人或许都不可避免地变得比平常更为野蛮、低智且暴力。

在这样的语境下大概不难理解，为什么规训技术可以称得上是现代社会的一项伟大发明，而为什么我们试图在此论述“原子化”是其中的核心——如果乌合之众的聚集很大概率会带来混乱和失控，那么，似乎确实只有把他们相互之间隔离起来，放进一个个可被预测的小格子里面，他们才有可能进一步变得有序与文明；惟其才可能使人类原本野蛮、冲动而尚武的肉体变成有生产力和具体功用的劳动力。惟在此时，群众那种可怕的潜在能量才被压制住了。

事实上，福柯在《全景敞视主义》之前的章节《断头台的场面》中就已经提到了这种“骚动的人群”对于君主权力的巨大潜在威胁。通过对犯人公开的残酷处刑，君主确实向治下的人民宣示/炫耀了无可辩驳的至高权力，但在另一个层面，这种行为又更深层次地抽拔出了一种临时的例外状态——此时，因为已经将要毫无疑问地赴死，作为“声名狼藉者”的犯人被允许在最后的几分钟里肆无忌惮地咒骂君王、法律与宗教，而通过热烈的喝彩和叫嚣，观看的群众在一定程度也是这种短暂反抗的参与者。在场面“辉煌”的断头台前，每一个人都意识到了在此般驾驭着生命的、无与伦比的权力和不受限制的合法暴力面前，自己注定的无力和渺小，这也就在无形中深刻团结了共同目睹着死刑“盛典”的个体们。
 
“断头台的场面”即是在仪式化和纪念性的场合，由多数人围观着拥有特权的一小撮人的权力表演；而“全景敞视主义”即是变做了在日常生活的每一天，由拥有特权的一小撮人监视着多数人。显然，对于权力的拥有者来说，前者还是太危险了，它在一些时候甚至会促成革命的发生；后者无疑更为高明，它高效且更可持续。前现代到现代的权力展示也就由之发生了伟大的转向。

“挤作一团的人群、多重交流的场所、混在一起的个性、集体效应被消除了，被一种隔离的个性的集合所取代。”

福柯曾多次表示过自己受到尼采哲学的强烈影响。尼采在《论道德的谱系》中书写的“自然人（#homo natura#）”与所谓“群盲/群氓”确实可以很好地为“监狱的诞生”添上注脚。在那个原始的自然状态中，人类是心血来潮、不顾后果、尊崇强者的丛林游戏玩家，是“瞬时情绪和欲念的奴隶”，是对弱者生杀予夺的“一伙金毛食肉动物”。在那种景况下，生命是污秽的、野兽般的、短促的。为了防止我们跌入这样不幸的“无休无止的战争状态”当中，我们一定需要对这种粗粝野蛮的原始人性施加管制，必须要有文明的秩序的驯服——按尼采的话讲，为人们穿上“社会的紧身衣”。

3. 一项既优美又阴险的方案

由之，两种状态被对立起来了——一方面是自然、原始、自由聚集却也有潜在的骚动、低智、暴力危险的状态，一方面是现代、文明、驯顺却也孤绝和压抑的状态。当杰里米·边沁意识到了这道选择题的存在，他给出了自己的答案。

“改良道德，保护健康，振兴工业，普及教育，减轻公共负担……这些通过一个简单的建筑理念就都可以实现！

Morals reformed-health preserved-industry invigorated-instruction diffused-public burthens lightened-Economy seated, as it were, upon a rock-the gordian knot of the Poor-Laws not cut, but untied-all by a simple idea in Architecture!”

对于一个以功利主义哲学辐射后世的社会改良家，边沁认为社会进步的最高目的只有也只能是一个——实现“最大多数人的最大幸福”，而这就是现代福利国家的核心要旨。

但这种观想显然是由似乎可以定量的“快乐”和“痛苦”的演算来成就的伦理学，也就是说，他为上述那道选择题（强行）赋予了一个答案。这是一种现在看来充满危险的倾向——原来，一些东西可以牺牲，只要一些更重要的“快乐”可以实现。在圆形监狱这个方案中，这项加减法的计算无比明显。“人民的自由精神和活力”被牺牲了，换取的则是“人民的温顺、安宁与秩序”。因为对边沁来讲，后者才代表了“最大多数人的利益”，即便它的代价是监视、隔离、精神奴役和心灵控制。

“……一个自由公民的自由精神和活力，是否会被士兵的机械纪律，或僧侣式的苦修所取代?——这种高度精巧的发明，其结果是否可能是制造出了一套近似人类的机器？

……在这样的准则下，幸福究竟是增加了还是减少了？——叫他们士兵也罢，叫他们僧侣也罢，叫他们机器也罢：只要他们幸福，我就不会在乎。

...whether the liberal spirit and energy of a free citizen would not be exchanged for the mechanical discipline of a soldier, or the austerity of a monk? - and whether the result of this high-wrought contrivance might not be constructing a set of machines under the similitude of men? ...Would happiness be most likely to be increased or diminished by this discipline? - Call them soldiers, call them monks, call them machines: so they were but happy ones, I should not care. 

——边沁，《圆形监狱》，第四章”

可以说，这一空间样板当初被提出时，似乎就已经自带了乌托邦与反乌托邦的双重性质。这也是为什么福柯会将之描述为“一种残酷而精巧的铁笼”，而为什么福柯传记的写作詹姆斯·米勒（James Miller）在真正理解了这项权力技术的奥妙之后，会由衷感叹它“既毋庸置疑地优美，又毋庸置疑地阴险。”

福柯所做出的一项极重要的事是指出了这条道路一种此前似乎被轻视的风险。在文章开头，我们提到了“全景敞视主义”作为一项诊断书，其面向的问题大致可以措辞为：既然现代社会看起来如此井然有序、亮丽美好，那么，为什么其中这么多人感到无比焦虑和抑郁？

综上，大概可以这样简述福柯的回应：从前的权力表现在于惩罚，譬如公开凌迟处死的盛大场面，而这代表了人类动物性的自然冲动和残酷快感的宣泄；从前的惩罚在于“对光线的剥夺”，它让囚犯像虫豸一样无尊严地活着，而现在的规训则在于“对黑暗的剥夺”，它使得人们永远无法在真正私密的黑暗中得到休憩。

当这种针对肉体的惩罚场面逐渐转变成了温和的规训和精密计算后的控制，这种暴力的减少并不单纯意味着人类整体道德的伟大提升。福柯，延续着他所私淑的尼采哲学论证，提醒我们，这种从暴力惩罚到温和规训的转向，这种对自然原始状态的背离，这种人类无法再释放到外部的本能的“内向化”，最终“引起了最重大、最难测的变态”，而这种“压抑下的病态”也就是现代人常常感到烦闷、焦虑、抑郁和痛苦的本质原因。


4. 伟大的抽象社会比喻

《就惩罚性监禁问题与福柯的会谈》上，福柯表示这种普遍的监视制度是“顺应新的形式而产生的”。

在《全景敞视主义》原文中可以拆解出下面几个显著的方面：

一，18-19世纪人口猛增。在这种情况下，从前过度的、浪费的、炫耀权力的统治模式变得“代价太高”，所以，不论是封建制、君主制或是地方监督机制都变得不适用了。全景敞视主义这种规训技术显得尤其经济而高效；

二，18-19世纪工业革命与资本主义兴起。在这种情况下，从前传统的、讲究仪式的、粗暴的管理模式不再实用。全景敞视主义这种规训技术作为一种高超的生产机构，带来了无处不在的“纪律”和“监督”，从而可以把原本混乱的“乌合之众”快速转化为有序的“劳动力”。所以工业革命、资本主义与新的规训技术相辅相成；

三，18-19世纪的“启蒙运动”提出了自由、平等、民主的法律框架。在这种情况下， “原则上的”法律形式需要一个“实质上的”微观权力进行维持。所以，原本“签字画押”的契约关系不再适用了，“纪律”这种强制关系才能扮演法律的基础设施。当然，这之间存在一个巨大的矛盾——上层的法律形式讲究平等，但下层的、贯彻它的“纪律”所带来的人际关系却是不平等和不对称的。人们仍旧与原则相悖的微观权力，是因为担心舍弃它之后找不到替代品。

四，18-19世纪许多学科知识增长。在这种情况下，全景敞视主义显然不只是在法律和工厂派上用场，它还进一步跨进了医院和学校。这种规训技术为现代社会中的人们规定了一个清楚的“正常状态”——要拥有驯顺的身体、驯顺的精神以及驯顺的知识。所以，现代意义上的“临床医学、精神病学、儿童心理学、教育心理学”等等相继出现，它们都可以被理解为规训技术在知识界的发明。


5. 被弱化的实际建成意义

然而许多时候有一点被忽略了——“全景敞视主义”作为一种空间样板或比喻，它毋庸置疑地伟大；但当“圆形监狱”作为一个实际建筑项目，它却并不十分成功，或者至少，随着时间推移，这些实际项目逐渐被弃用。

在纸上，这项方案永远是有效和有力的。20世纪的激进建筑师团体创造过大量富于张力的讽喻性寓言，这些图像故事当中许多都找得到“全景敞视主义”直接或间接的影子。譬如在超级工作室（Superstudio）的《12个圣诞节警世故事（#Twelve Cautionary Tales for Christmas#）》（也译作“十二座理想之城”）的第一个《2000吨之城》。

在这个短小的故事中，建筑物是连绵的巨大尺度方格网，每个居民都住在一间间“方形巢室”里。其令人不寒而栗之处在于——安装在天花板上的分析仪会不断“挑选、比较、综合每一个个体的期望，时时刻刻为整座城市规划出一种生活模式”，“确保所有市民永远在相同条件的环境中生活。”这里没有死亡，所有的需求也得到满足，但如果一个人想要有反抗，“天花板屏幕会以2000吨重力下压，直到与地板完全密合。”这种制度带给个体的同质化，这样的系统对于个体反抗的防范，不正像是“圆形监狱”提案的一次改写？

此时，一个值得建筑师思忖的话题或许就在于，这个在纸上极其强有力、发人深省的方案，走进现实之后如何？

在现在的语境下，或许正因为这个概念作为整体被抽象化了，它作为建筑项目本身的价值也就受到了架空；当“panopticon/panopticism”越发成为学术热词，一个应当被讨论，但并没有被足够讨论的问题是——边沁所设想的全景敞视式的圆形监狱，到底有没有被建成并投入使用过？换句话说，这个概念一开始诞生时所面向的局面——当监狱真的按照边沁提案那样建造，这样的建筑到底好不好用？

首先可以确定的是，杰里米·边沁至死也没有看见过自己所骄傲的方案实际建成。其次，即便他的身后有不少形似圆环的建成物，但“圆形监狱是否曾在历史中被建成使用过”这一点仍无确论。

简单来说，在英国、意大利、荷兰、西班牙、俄罗斯、美国、古巴、南非、澳大利亚等地，近两百年间确有不少实际建成的监狱在形态上酷肖边沁所提出的原型。确实，这些封闭而割裂的囚室都分布在一个圆周上。但一个值得引起注意的质疑是，这些建成案例并没有精确依照边沁主张中的关键——“全景敞视”，也就是说，中心的瞭望塔并没有在囚犯心理上造成持续监视的威压。

譬如在都柏林的凯勒梅汉姆监狱（Kilmainham Gaol）中，中心的大厅确实拥有全景而开敞的视野，但并未设置瞭望与监视的设备与房间；在荷兰的科佩尔圆形监狱（Koepel Panopticon Prison）中，中心大厅确有瞭望塔，但它在建成不久后实际上就被改造成了狱警的小餐室——“看-被看”倒置了，狱警观察囚犯服刑变成了囚犯观察狱警用餐。

要么并未设置中心瞭望塔，要么瞭望塔被改造成了小餐室。许多实际建造的圆形监狱里，“全景敞视”的理念是名存实亡的。

此外，许多其他类似建成物即便没有拆除中心的瞭望塔，但监狱在实际运转的过程中同样未曾严格遵循边沁当初对于建筑使用的说明。随着时间的推进，它们中的很大部分都被渐渐弃用，不少被转化为了博物馆或其他用途。

对这种现象的反思大多集中在四点。

首先，作为实际建成项目，圆形监狱的空间使用效率并不十分理想。由于它需要中心的瞭望塔与外侧的禁闭室之间存在足够长的距离，这之间巨大的面积几乎都是空置的。

其次，圆形监狱中狱警/服刑人员的人数比例过低。监狱作为政府的暴力机关，需要保证狱警能够在任何可能的情况下压制住服刑人员们。圆形监狱确实大大降低了人力成本，但是这也导致狱警和服刑人员人数的悬殊比例。在一些特殊的但仍可能的场合下，罪犯们如果发起暴动、群起攻之，圆形监狱中极少的狱警人员将难以招架。

第三，圆形监狱提倡的对服刑人员“无死角的压制”不再适应现代社会的人伦语境。边沁提倡其空间能无死角地压制和监视服刑人员，但现代监狱系统在这方面已有转向，它需要保证服刑人员们拥有一定放风时间和相互沟通的机会。崇尚绝对无死角和隔离的空间模式显然在新时代下存在问题。

但最为重要的是，相比于边沁的时代，在21世纪，很多建筑理念的实现并不再严格依赖于现实空间了。譬如说圆形监狱中起关键作用的“看-被看”关系，在18-20世纪，这或许真的只能通过“中心瞭望塔-外围禁闭室”的实体构筑物来实现。但在数百年后的今天，技术的革新使得“看-被看”只需要在每个房间加装一个不到拳头大小的监视器。在边沁的时代，若想要向民众彰示权力的在场与威压，最好的方式是建造诸如“凯旋门”这样的超尺度、象征性的建筑物；但在今天，权力的在场与威压或许是通过“钉钉”这样的App交互设计得以实现的。

当权力所需要的舞台从实体建筑转向了虚拟的互联世界，具体的管教场所还是否沿用圆形监狱的形式就不再重要了。因为权力的所有方早已有更轻盈、更无形却也更具渗透性的意识形态武器来完成从前只有砖混巨物才能达成的成效。

在这一点上我们或许可以重新回到“圆形监狱是否投入使用过”这一辩题上，因为当这个方案去实体化以后，它仍与边沁最初的主张有相悖之处。假想的环形排列的囚室中，服刑者必须随时随地主观意识到“凝视者”的存在；但在今天的网络环境中，“凝视者”会尽量弱化自己的存在，而试图在用户不经意间收集数据、引导行为。

从18世纪的社会改良方案，到20世纪对于西方社会的批判，再到21世纪具备世界性意义的讨论话语，这项空间样板在不同的时代语境下变形着不同的、甚至自悖的意义。它作为一个词汇持续不断被使用，并且持续扩展着在多种学科领域和实际、虚拟项目中的意义。人们可以质疑它模糊的多义性，质疑它不同方面的权重，质疑它在许多时候无法“精确适用”，但几乎无人质疑这个概念不是重要的。建筑学、社会学、政治学、传播学等等领域的学者高频谈论着它，因为这个词在几乎所有时候都保持了对于社会最重大、最基本问题的敏感，这是一把由边沁、福柯以及后来者们锻造出来的强有力的理论武器和思维工具。

在福柯笔下，监狱是整个现代社会的建筑原型。在这个基础上，精神病院、工厂、学校、办公室等等，不外乎也是圆形监狱的某种变形。叫它改良也好，称其教化也罢，现代社会的核心要义似乎就在于规范了一个人应有的“正常状态”，然后不断确保人们生长成那个样子。

分配——监视——隔离，充满活力的、骚动的、不可控的自然人被改造成了温顺的、有序的、具备生产力的现代人。一项乌托邦在被写就的刹那起，其反乌托邦的性质就已从自身中衍生出来；“全景敞视”曾代表18世纪社会进步的倡议，也在人类被愈演愈烈的制度化笼盖时，显出了它控制、压抑、奴役的另一面象征。

“凝视”与心灵压迫之外，这项方案不应被忽视的另一个方面是它对个体流动和聚合的可能性的封锁。实际上，如果我们再度回到《全景敞视主义》一章的开篇，福柯的论述正是由瘟疫横行下的社区封闭和管制开始的；这样高压的统筹如果变成了常态，那一定是可怖的现实。无疑，这样的篇章对于时空相隔遥远的当今世界来说，有巨大的预言、警示和反思价值。

content.en:
The Panopticon is also translated as the #round prison#. As one of the most pervasive concepts in architecture, our interpretation aims to highlight two primary issues. This article was originally published in June 2020 on the WeChat official account of #Dunes Workshop#—
First, "panopticism" is not merely discipline under surveillance; it is the suppression of collective mobility. Second, while the "Panopticon" has been an immense success as a spatial archetype or social metaphor, its value as an actual built project remains relatively mediocre.
The original text follows:
How do you turn a group of savages into modern citizens? Step one: Place them in individual cubicles; Step two: Ensure they know their behavior is constantly being monitored; Step three: Isolate them to ensure they cannot form a crowd.
The aforementioned process of reform or edification can serve as a simplified summary of "panopticism" in Michel Foucault’s #Discipline and Punish#.
1. As Manifesto or Diagnosis
As an unconventional thinker, Foucault’s writing is often "easy to sense but difficult to pin down." This technology of power—or spatial archetype—seems to be both an instruction manual and a medical diagnosis. Its significance as a manual responds to the question posed at the beginning: How can a restless, savage, and impulsive "mob" be transformed into orderly, manageable, and productive modern subjects? As a diagnosis, it addresses a different question: Since modern society appears so orderly, polished, and beautiful, why do so many within it feel such profound anxiety and depression?
If we return to the original text where the concept was proposed, it is easy to see that Jeremy Bentham’s 1787 essay, #Panopticon: or the Inspection House#, was clearly intended as an instruction manual—a proposal, a design, a Utopian vision. (Strictly speaking, Jeremy Bentham’s brother, Samuel Bentham, was the first to propose the "Panopticon" after observing the "central inspection principle" in Russian factories. Jeremy Bentham later adapted this principle into his prison proposal.) In contrast, Foucault’s #Discipline and Punish#, written nearly 200 years later, emerged as a diagnosis. Especially in the chapter titled #Panopticism#, the French scholar unearthed the prison scheme envisioned by the British jurist and pointed out with surgical precision that Bentham’s "reformatory"—when viewed not as a strictly built project but as an abstract modality—had become the overarching condition of Western modern society. Far more than just prisons, the "panoptic model" has been widely applied to psychiatric hospitals, factories, schools, and offices. Thus, through Foucault’s reintroduction in the 1970s, the "Panopticon" as a discourse became a chilling, dystopian social critique. Today’s architectural circles and the broader academic world continue to follow Foucault’s textual interpretation. When we use this concept, we essentially treat it as a synonym for "white terror" and "mental enslavement," referring to the unfortunate plight of modern individuals controlled by authority and manipulated by rules.
2. The Panopticon Dissolves the Scene of Gathering
This prestigious academic concept has entered public discussion with increasing frequency due to its highly accurate description of social reality. However, it should be noted that many interpretations of "panopticism" today seem somewhat narrow—people are often more fascinated by the "Big Brother is watching you" aspect of this spatial model, which is the second step in our simplified scenario.
Understandably, the roots of the word "panopticon"—"pan-" (all) and "optic" (seeing)—combine to mean "all-seeing," which is structurally similar to "omniscient" (from "omni-," all, and "scire," to know).
Thus, the word itself emphasizes the status of the central watchtower. Consequently, many discussions detail how individuals, under the constant gaze, dare not deviate from the rules, to the point where they continue "self-gazing" and "self-managing" even when the supervisor is absent. In the contemporary world, perhaps because of dense surveillance systems and ubiquitous censorship, writers primarily use this classic "seeing and being seen" relationship of the Panopticon to interpret reality.
But this is not the entirety of "panopticism."
"He is seen, but he does not see; he is the object of information, never a subject in communication." Foucault noted that the arrangement of the room facing the central tower creates centripetal visibility, but the division into cells means a "lateral invisibility."
Another equally, if not more, important element is the third step of our simplified scenario: in the Panopticon, every individual is cast into a state of absolute isolation. They cannot communicate smoothly, they cannot huddle, and they cannot coalesce into a so-called "group." Therefore, this technology of power ensures that these individuals always remain the passive party in a hierarchy, unable to reverse the relationship. From the perspective of communicative theory, it causes "discourse" to perish and dissolves the possibility of a public sphere.
Why must people be scattered? Why must they be prevented from gathering to form a public? We might return to Bentham’s era. At the end of the 18th century, the jurist was so enthusiastic about his brilliant scheme that he traveled everywhere to pitch it. He was not a "mad evil scientist," and his spatial vision was clearly not born of pure "evil" intent. On the contrary, Bentham viewed it as a benign "reformatory." He envisioned a place where morbid, deviant, and criminal individuals and thoughts would be reformed by concepts of order, reason, and morality—a catalytic chamber leading us toward civilization.
The scene of people connecting and gathering always alarms those in power because, compared to scattered individuals, a group is "powerful." We also need to understand that the "masses" formed by gathering individuals are not always noble, moral, or selfless. When individuals come together, a distinct "group spirit" seems to take over, releasing a certain restless animal energy that is usually suppressed.
"The democratic power of the masses, like all individual power, easily turns into its opposite—a tyrannical power—when not subject to proper constitutional constraints." At such moments, "moral constraints and civilized modes in thought and feeling suddenly vanish, and primitive impulses, infantile behaviors, and criminal tendencies erupt." In other words, once individuals aggregate into a crowd, each person may inevitably become more savage, less intelligent, and more violent than usual.
In this context, it is not hard to understand why disciplinary technology can be called a great invention of modern society, and why we argue that "atomization" is its core. If the gathering of a "mob" is likely to bring chaos and loss of control, then isolating them into predictable "cubicles" seems to be the only way they might become orderly and civilized. Only then can the originally savage, impulsive, and martial human body be transformed into productive and useful labor. Only then is the terrifying potential energy of the masses suppressed.
In fact, in the chapter preceding #Panopticism#, "The Spectacle of the Scaffold," Foucault mentioned the great potential threat that this "restless crowd" posed to sovereign power. Through the public and brutal execution of prisoners, the sovereign did display indisputable supreme power. However, on another level, this act extracted a temporary "state of exception"—at this moment, knowing they were to die, the "infamous" prisoner was allowed to recklessly curse the king, the law, and religion in their final minutes. Through fervent cheers and clamor, the watching crowd became, to an extent, participants in this brief resistance. Before the "splendid" scaffold, everyone realized their destined impotence and insignificance in the face of such life-dominating power and unrestricted legal violence, which invisibly but deeply united the individuals witnessing the "festival" of death.
"The Spectacle of the Scaffold" is a ritualized and monumental occasion where the many watch the power performance of a privileged few; "Panopticism" is its inversion—the daily surveillance of the many by a privileged few. Clearly, for those in power, the former was too dangerous; it could even catalyze revolution. The latter is undoubtedly more sophisticated, efficient, and sustainable. Thus, a great shift occurred in the display of power from the pre-modern to the modern era.
"The crowd, a compact mass, a locus of multiple exchanges, individualities merging together, a collective effect, is abolished and replaced by a collection of separated individualities."
Foucault often stated he was strongly influenced by Nietzsche’s philosophy. The "natural man" (#homo natura#) and the so-called "herd" described by Nietzsche in #On the Genealogy of Morals# provide an excellent footnote to "the birth of the prison." In that original state of nature, humans were impulsive, reckless players in a jungle game, "slaves to momentary emotions and desires," a "pack of blond beasts of prey" with the power of life and death over the weak. In such circumstances, life was nasty, brutish, and short. To prevent us from falling into this unfortunate "ceaseless state of war," we must regulate this raw, savage human nature with the domesticating order of civilization—or as Nietzsche put it, put people in a "social straitjacket."
3. A Scheme Both Beautiful and Insidious
Consequently, two states are polarized—on one hand, the natural, primitive, and free state of gathering with its inherent dangers of chaos and violence; on the other, the modern, civilized, and docile state, which is also isolated and repressed. When Jeremy Bentham realized this choice existed, he gave his answer.
"Morals reformed—health preserved—industry invigorated—instruction diffused—public burthens lightened... all by a simple idea in Architecture!"
As a social reformer whose utilitarian philosophy influenced subsequent generations, Bentham believed the ultimate goal of social progress was the "greatest happiness of the greatest number," which is the core tenet of the modern welfare state.
But this vision is clearly an ethics achieved through the calculus of quantifiable "pleasure" and "pain." He (forcibly) provided an answer to the aforementioned choice. This is a tendency that seems dangerous today—the idea that some things can be sacrificed as long as a more important "happiness" is achieved. In the Panopticon scheme, this addition and subtraction is glaringly obvious. The "liberal spirit and energy of the people" are sacrificed in exchange for "docility, tranquility, and order." For Bentham, the latter represented the "interest of the greatest number," even if the price was surveillance, isolation, and mental enslavement.
"...whether the liberal spirit and energy of a free citizen would not be exchanged for the mechanical discipline of a soldier, or the austerity of a monk? — and whether the result of this high-wrought contrivance might not be constructing a set of machines under the similitude of men? ...Would happiness be most likely to be increased or diminished by this discipline? — Call them soldiers, call them monks, call them machines: so they were but happy ones, I should not care." — Bentham, #Panopticon#, Chapter 4.

It can be said that when this spatial model was proposed, it inherently possessed a dual nature of Utopia and Dystopia. This is why Foucault described it as a "cruel, ingenious cage," and why Foucault’s biographer, James Miller, upon truly understanding the subtlety of this power technology, remarked that it was "at once indubitably beautiful and indubitably insidious."
One of the most important things Foucault did was point out a risk in this path that had previously been overlooked. At the beginning of the article, we mentioned "panopticism" as a diagnosis. The problem it addresses can be phrased as: Since modern society looks so orderly and beautiful, why do so many feel so anxious and depressed?
In summary, Foucault’s response can be simplified as follows: Former power was expressed through punishment, such as the grand spectacle of public execution, which represented the venting of natural animal impulses and cruel pleasure. Former punishment lay in the "deprivation of light," making prisoners live without dignity like insects. Modern discipline, however, lies in the "deprivation of darkness," ensuring people can never rest in truly private darkness.
As the spectacle of corporal punishment gradually transformed into mild discipline and calculated control, this reduction in violence did not simply mean a great leap in overall human morality. Foucault, following the Nietzschean tradition, reminds us that this shift from violent punishment to mild discipline—this departure from the natural state and the "interiorization" of instincts that can no longer be released outwardly—eventually "caused the most serious and most subterranean sickness." This "pathology of repression" is the essence of why modern people often feel bored, anxious, depressed, and pained.
4. A Great Abstract Social Metaphor
In #The Punitive Society#, Foucault stated that this universal system of surveillance "arose to meet new forms."
In the original text of #Panopticism#, several distinct aspects can be deconstructed:
Population Explosion: In the 18th and 19th centuries, the population surged. Under these circumstances, the former excessive, wasteful, and ostentatious modes of sovereign power became "too costly." Whether feudalism, monarchy, or local supervision, they were no longer applicable. Panopticism, as a disciplinary technology, proved exceptionally economical and efficient.
The Industrial Revolution and the Rise of Capitalism: Traditional, ritualistic, and crude management modes were no longer practical. Panopticism, as a sophisticated production apparatus, brought ubiquitous "discipline" and "supervision," quickly transforming the chaotic "mob" into an orderly "labor force." Thus, the Industrial Revolution, capitalism, and new disciplinary technologies complemented one another.
The Enlightenment and the Legal Framework: The Enlightenment proposed a legal framework of liberty, equality, and democracy. In this context, "principled" legal forms required a "substantial" micro-power to maintain them. The old contract-based relationships were no longer sufficient; "discipline" as a coercive relationship became the infrastructure of the law. Of course, a massive contradiction exists here—the macro legal forms stress equality, but the micro-power of discipline is inherently unequal and asymmetrical. People cling to this contradictory micro-power for fear of finding no alternative.
Growth of Disciplines: Panopticism was applied beyond law and factories into hospitals and schools. This technology defined a "normal state" for modern people—requiring a docile body, a docile spirit, and docile knowledge. Thus, "clinical medicine, psychiatry, child psychology, and educational psychology" emerged as inventions of disciplinary technology in the intellectual sphere.
5. The Diminished Significance of the Built Reality
However, one point is often overlooked: while "panopticism" is undoubtedly great as a spatial archetype or metaphor, the "Panopticon" as an actual architectural project was not very successful. Over time, these physical projects were gradually abandoned.
On paper, the scheme is eternally effective. 20th-century radical architectural groups created many tension-filled allegories, many of which contain direct or indirect shadows of "panopticism." For example, in Superstudio’s #Twelve Cautionary Tales for Christmas# (also translated as #Twelve Ideal Cities#), the first tale is #The City of the 2,000-Ton Slab#.
In this short story, the building is a continuous, massive grid where every resident lives in a "square cell." The chilling part is that analyzers installed in the ceiling constantly "select, compare, and synthesize the desires of every individual, planning a life pattern for the entire city at every moment," ensuring all citizens live in identical conditions. There is no death, and all needs are met, but if someone tries to rebel, "the ceiling screen will press down with 2,000 tons of gravity until it meets the floor." Is this homogenization and prevention of resistance not a rewriting of the "Panopticon" proposal?
At this point, a topic for architects to ponder is: how does this scheme, so powerful and thought-provoking on paper, fare in reality?
In the current context, perhaps because the concept has been abstracted as a whole, its value as an architectural project has been hollowed out. While "panopticon/panopticism" becomes an academic buzzword, an under-discussed question is: Was the panoptic round prison envisioned by Bentham ever actually built and used? In other words, did the building actually work well when constructed according to Bentham’s proposal?
First, it is certain that Jeremy Bentham never saw his proud scheme built during his lifetime. Second, although many ring-shaped buildings appeared after his death, there is no consensus on whether a "Panopticon" was ever truly operated according to his principles.
In short, while many prisons in the UK, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Russia, the US, Cuba, South Africa, and Australia resembled Bentham’s prototype over the last 200 years, critics argue they did not accurately implement the key element: "Panopticism." That is, the central watchtower did not create a psychological pressure of constant surveillance on the prisoners.
For instance, in Dublin’s #Kilmainham Gaol#, the central hall has a panoramic view but lacks surveillance equipment. In the Netherlands’ #Koepel Panopticon Prison#, the central tower existed, but it was soon converted into a small canteen for guards—the "seeing-being seen" relationship was inverted: instead of guards watching prisoners, prisoners watched guards eat.
Either there was no central tower, or the tower became a canteen. In many physical Panopticons, the concept of "Panopticism" existed in name only. Furthermore, even where towers remained, the prisons rarely followed Bentham’s strict operational instructions. Most were eventually abandoned or converted into museums.
Reflections on this phenomenon focus on four points:
Spatial Inefficiency: As a built project, the Panopticon’s efficiency is poor. Because it requires a significant distance between the tower and the cells, the vast area in between is mostly wasted space.
Low Guard-to-Inmate Ratio: As a state apparatus of violence, a prison must ensure guards can suppress inmates in any situation. While the Panopticon reduced labor costs, it led to a precarious ratio. In riots, the few guards would be easily overwhelmed.
Conflict with Modern Ethics: Bentham’s "total suppression" no longer fits modern human rights contexts. Modern systems require inmates to have recreation time and communication opportunities. A model of absolute isolation is problematic in the new era.
Virtualization of Power: Most importantly, in the 21st century, architectural concepts no longer rely strictly on physical space. The "seeing-being seen" relationship that once required a massive stone structure now only requires a camera smaller than a fist. In Bentham’s time, to show the presence of power, one built a #Triumphal Arch#; today, power is felt through the interface design of apps like DingTalk.
When the stage of power shifts from physical buildings to the virtual world, the specific form of the disciplinary site becomes less important. Those in power have lighter, invisible, yet more pervasive ideological weapons to achieve what once required a masonry colossus.
Here, we return to the debate over whether the Panopticon was ever used. Once the scheme is de-physicalized, it still contradicts Bentham’s original claim. In the hypothetical ring of cells, the inmate must be consciously aware of the "gazer." In today’s network environment, the "gazer" hides their presence, collecting data and guiding behavior while the user is unaware.
From an 18th-century reform plan to 20th-century Western social critique to a 21st-century global discourse, this spatial archetype has morphed into different, even self-contradictory meanings. As a term, it is used continuously across disciplines. One can question its ambiguity or its applicability, but few can deny its importance. Scholars in architecture, sociology, politics, and communications talk about it because it remains sensitive to the most fundamental social issues—a powerful theoretical weapon forged by Bentham, Foucault, and those who followed.
In Foucault’s writing, the prison is the architectural prototype of modern society. On this basis, psychiatric hospitals, factories, schools, and offices are merely variations of the Panopticon. Whether you call it reform or edification, the core of modern society seems to lie in defining a "normal state" and ensuring people grow into that mold.
Distribution—Surveillance—Isolation. The vibrant, restless, uncontrollable natural man is transformed into a docile, orderly, productive modern subject. From the moment a Utopia is written, its dystopian nature is born. "Panopticism," once a proposal for social progress in the 18th century, revealed its other side—control, repression, and enslavement—as humanity became increasingly enveloped by institutionalization.
Beyond "the gaze" and mental oppression, another aspect of this scheme that should not be ignored is its blockage of individual movement and the possibility of gathering. Indeed, if we return to the beginning of the #Panopticism# chapter, Foucault’s discussion begins with the closure and regulation of communities during a plague. If such high-pressure coordination becomes the norm, it is a terrifying reality. Undoubtedly, such chapters hold immense prophetic, cautionary, and reflective value for today’s world, regardless of the distance in time and space.

brief_definition.zh: 基于反馈机制的调节原理
brief_definition.en: Feedback-based regulatory principle

zh: 想象你是一名船长，驾驶着一艘船在海上航行，你的目标就在笔直的前方。然而，你不能扶住舵不动就抵达终点，而是需要不断观察风向、洋流、波浪等等因素——输入一个指令，观察环境对船的影响如何，再输入下一个指令。就像是中文的俗语“走一步看一步”。这就是“控制论”（cybernetic）的基本意涵，它的词源正是希腊语中“舵手” （#kybernētēs#）一词。
柏拉图在《理想国》里曾用“掌舵”这一比喻来阐释对人民的管理。控制论之父维纳认为，这一比喻最好地展现了“反馈”这一控制论的机制，因此在英语中复用了这一希腊语词汇。在一个反馈机制里，行动者观察到的自己采取行动的结果，这一观察成为影响进一步行动的因素，从而形成一种循环或递归的因果关系。反馈机制在生物学、社会学等几乎所有学科中都有不同的展现和应用。
“控制论”是认知科学、计算机科学、信息理论、人工智能等领域的基础。不过在社会研究中，“控制论”有批判意义，它指出了环境因素左右着个体意志的状况。
en: Imagine you are a captain sailing a ship across the sea, with your destination lying straight ahead. However, you cannot simply hold the rudder steady and expect to arrive; instead, you must constantly observe factors such as wind direction, currents, and waves—issuing a command, observing how the environment affects the ship, and then adjusting with the next command. It is much like the Chinese proverb, "taking one step and looking around before the next." This is the fundamental meaning of "cybernetics," a term whose etymology traces back to the Greek word for "steersman" (kybernētēs).

Plato, in The Republic, employed the metaphor of "steering" to elucidate the governance of a people. Norbert Wiener, the father of cybernetics, believed this metaphor best illustrated the mechanism of "feedback"; hence, he resurrected this Greek root in English. In a feedback mechanism, the actor observes the results of their own actions, and this observation becomes a factor influencing further action, thereby creating a circular or recursive causal relationship. Feedback mechanisms manifest in diverse forms across nearly all disciplines, including biology and sociology.

"Cybernetics" serves as the bedrock for fields such as cognitive science, computer science, information theory, and artificial intelligence. However, within social studies, it carries a critical connotation: it highlights a condition where environmental factors govern and steer individual will.

example_sentence.zh: 在自媒体平台上，创作者收到的数据反馈常常成为他们生产下一个内容的影响因素，这种实时的“控制论”机制导致了严重的同质化。
example_sentence.en: On social media platforms, the data feedback creators receive often becomes the primary factor influencing their next piece of content. This real-time "cybernetic" mechanism has led to severe homogenization.

content.zh: 这个创作过程的变化并不是直接受迫的，而是在“赛博世界”受自己能动性驱使的，这仿佛完全“自主”和“自愿”。
content.en: This shift in the creative process was not the result of direct coercion; rather, it was driven by their own agency within the "cyber-world." It feels entirely "autonomous" and "voluntary."

content.zh:
“Cybernetics”的词根是希腊语“kybernetes”，意思是“掌舵人”。我们可以想象这样一幅场景：茫茫海上，小船在波涛上航行，掌舵人控制着船的行驶。他根据自己的意志调节着前进的方向，而前进的同时，波浪不断拍打着船只，这些环境的因素又不断影响着他下一步对方向的判断。

这一场景大致描绘出了控制论的核心：根据系统反馈进行的自我控制。当我们把它放在传播系统里的时候，我们能看见，例如——要是上传到B站的视频播发量低、弹幕少、反响寥寥，Up主自己会想办法去提高播发量，他可以调整自己选题的内容，剪辑的方式，或者砍掉某个不太受欢迎的栏目，此后，上传新的一条视频内容，观察反响的变化，继续做出调整。在这个“控制论”的系统里，并不是市场、政府或者领导直接下达命令，告诉创作者什么应该做，什么不应该做，而是创作者不断通过“输入-得到反馈-调整-再输入”的迭代过程为自己施加的“自我控制”。假使这位Up主在入驻B站两年以后，内容从选题到风格都已经全然偏离了自己最初的意愿，这个创作过程的变化并不是直接受迫的，而是在“赛博世界”受自己能动性驱使的，这仿佛完全“自主”和“自愿”。
content.en:
The etymological root of "Cybernetics" is the Greek word "kybernetes," meaning "steersman" or "helmsman." We might imagine a scene like this: amidst a vast sea, a small boat navigates the waves as the helmsman controls its course. He adjusts the direction of progress according to his own will; yet, as the boat moves forward, waves continuously batter the vessel. These environmental factors, in turn, constantly influence his judgment regarding the next directional adjustment.
This scene roughly sketches the core of cybernetics: self-control based on systemic feedback. When we apply this to communication systems, we can see it in action—for instance, if a video uploaded to Bilibili receives low view counts, sparse bullet chats, and a lackluster response, the creator (Uploader) will naturally find ways to increase engagement. They might adjust their topic selection, the style of editing, or even axe a poorly received segment. Subsequently, they upload a new piece of content, observe the change in response, and continue making adjustments.
Within this "cybernetic" system, it is not the market, the government, or a supervisor directly issuing orders to tell the creator what should or should not be done. Instead, it is a form of "self-control" imposed by the creators themselves through an iterative process of "input—receiving feedback—adjustment—re-input." Suppose that after two years on Bilibili, this creator’s content—from themes to style—has completely deviated from their original intent. This shift in the creative process was not the result of direct coercion; rather, it was driven by their own agency within the "cyber-world." It feels entirely "autonomous" and "voluntary."

brief_definition.zh: 指由于受到过多的外部刺激而产生的麻木、厌倦和冷漠态度
brief_definition.en: A state of numbness, boredom, and indifference resulting from exposure to excessive external stimuli.

zh: 东京涩谷的十字路口车辆穿梭，霓虹灯闪烁，成千上万张陌生的面孔在几秒钟内迎面扑来，随即消失。来自乡村的访客会被这巨大的感官洪流击倒，每一个声音、每一件商品都会引起他的注意和惊奇；而他身旁的本地人却对此视而不见，面无表情地匆匆走过。
20世纪初，工业技术的快速发展创造出当时前所未有的大都市，也催生了一种新的群体——都市人。相比于乡村慢节奏的熟人社会，复杂的都市中多样的外部刺激使都市人产生了一种漠然、无感的态度，以此保护自己不堪重负的精神。
齐美尔在提出“倦怠态度”的文章中，对比了都市与乡村的生活，从心理和精神层面剖析了都市人这一新兴群体。他指出，都市人用头脑（理性）取代心灵（情感），以应对过多的信息和刺激。同时，都市作为贸易中心，确立了精确与高效的现代精神。相比于紧密联系的乡土人情社会，都市人这种有所保留的态度，虽然使他们获得了更多的个体自由及独特性，但这种自由并非舒适的——即便无时无刻不处在人群中，他们仍然时常感到孤独和迷失。
en: At the Shibuya Crossing in Tokyo, traffic weaves through, neon lights flicker, and thousands of strange faces rush toward you and vanish within seconds. A visitor from the countryside would be overwhelmed by this immense sensory deluge; every sound and every commodity would spark their attention and wonder. Yet, the locals walk past with expressionless faces.

In the early 20th century, the rapid development of industrial technology created metropolises unprecedented at the time, and with them, a new demographic—the city dweller. Compared to the slow-paced society of acquaintances in the countryside, the diverse external stimuli of the complex city cause city dwellers to develop an attitude of indifference and insensitivity to protect their overloaded minds.

In his essay proposing the concept of the "blasé attitude," Simmel contrasted urban and rural life, dissecting this emerging group of city dwellers from a psychological and spiritual perspective. He pointed out that city dwellers react with their heads (intellect) instead of their hearts (emotions) to cope with the excess of information and stimuli. At the same time, the city as a center of trade established precision and efficiency as the modern spirit. Compared to the closely-knit rural society, the city dweller's attitude of reserve grants them greater individual freedom and uniqueness. However, this freedom is not necessarily comfortable; even when constantly surrounded by crowds, they still often feel lonely and lost.

example_sentence.zh: 社交媒体可被看作一种虚拟的“齐美尔式大都市”，上面刺激视听的消息几乎无穷无尽，这不免让很多用户产生了“倦怠态度”。
example_sentence.en: Social media can be viewed as a virtual "Simmelian metropolis," where the stream of audio-visual stimuli is nearly endless, inevitably leading many users to develop a "blasé attitude."

content.zh: 柏青哥店里面震耳欲聋的弹珠响，满座顾客一次一次拉动摇杆、屏幕动效疯狂闪烁，音效又一波盖过一波。第一次走进去，耳朵和眼睛都招架不住。同学转头说：“久了你会感觉这个反倒解压。”
content.en: Inside a Pachinko parlor, the clatter of silver balls is deafening. Rows of customers pull levers repeatedly while screen animations flash frantically, one sound effect drowning out the next. Stepping in for the first time, your ears and eyes simply can’t cope. My classmate turned and said, "After a while, you’ll find this actually relieves stress."

content.zh:
这篇文章于2023年11月发布在沙丘研究所的公众号上——

多年前第一次旅游东京，非常震悚于这个城市的密度。这个密度不只是说楼房和人口的密度，而是说一种整体都市性的密度——什么都塞到了最满。无数的图形和多种语言文字都着迫不及待地往人眼睛上拍。当时我没有那么多资本主义、景观社会的反思，被这种大城市的引力紧紧抓住，觉得什么都想看，什么东西都想注意。

和待在日本时间长的同学聊，她当即的反应就是：“这种感觉会过去的。”现在想来这个就是齐美尔说的“倦怠态度”。人不可能在东京待个十年，每天出门都还在对着那些街道大惊小怪。“倦怠”几乎成了一种必然的精神防御，防止人的大脑在过多刺激下过载。

柏青哥店里面震耳欲聋的弹珠响，满座顾客一次一次拉动摇杆、屏幕动效疯狂闪烁，音效又一波盖过一波。第一次走进去，耳朵和眼睛都招架不住。同学转头说：“久了你会感觉这个反倒解压。”看来日本社畜那层“倦怠”的壳果是要比我厚不少，抗药性强了，必须要把剂量加到这个程度才行。不过奇怪的是，最近一年我忽然有点理解了——客厅放着电视，我在房间里刷社交媒体，甚至还一边放着播客。奇怪的是，那种被媒介塞满的状态反而让人短时间里放空。John Mulaney在单口里面描述自己在纽约的状态：“我可能从2014年开始就一直处在神游中，像卓别林一样走进车流里面，耳朵里听着一档播客，脑子里又想着另一档播客。”一方面对各种刺激视听的东西见怪不怪，一方面身处其中不想离开，闲暇的时候又得靠过度剂量才觉得舒服，这个就是都市人的精神状况。

倦怠也指向为人处世上慢慢积养起来的厚壳。相比乡村熟人社会，在都市中生活的人会接触到多几十上百倍的陌生人，并和他们产生浅的深的交往。因为知道一些关系必然转瞬即逝，知道一些人不怀好意，或者有截然不同的利益取向，“都市人”养成的社交模式自然会转向世故、冷漠或者抽离。在大都市里逢人就交出真心，既无效率又容易受伤害。

我最后想要从人际上延伸的是一种伦理或者良知上的倦怠。路易CK在自嘲纽约人对待流浪汉的态度的时候说：“流浪汉也太多了，你得做出选择才行。你没法全都帮，当然，你也一个都不会帮。” 我更喜欢的是他的另一个段子。他讲他在纽约有个朋友，这个朋友有一个来自小地方的表妹。表妹第一次来到大城市纽约，显然还远没有习惯纽约街上流浪汉遍地的场景。两人刚在车站接到表妹，往外走着，这时女孩看到角落里一个浑身垃圾、臭气熏天的流浪汉，大骇，赶忙冲上前去，单膝跪在地上，着急地问：“先生，你怎么了？发生了什么？”这时候，路易CK和朋友也赶忙冲上去，拉住这个“天真的农村女孩”，“别别别，我们这儿不这么做！”

这种“纠正”当然很荒唐，但也非常说明问题。在一个污秽的人、事、物像漩涡般疯狂聚集的大都市里面，待久了的居民当然已经训练出视而不见的麻木品格。要是纽约客每天注目和过问每一件城市里发生的罪恶、不公和不幸，那自己的日子也完全没法过了。这近乎成了在这个地方生存的行为准则——于是，两人赶紧上前拉住了想要提供帮助的表妹，像是一个东道主教育客人的餐桌礼仪一样：“我们这里不这么做！”这也是倦怠的一种。

不得不提的是，如果说19世纪末现代大都市的出现，让社会学家齐美尔观察到了与之伴随的新的人，新的性格，新的精神的出现，那么对我们现在来说，社交媒体就是这样一个对等的，甚至更为极端的状况。不管是图像数量、刺激力度、接触到的人际数量，还是对于苦难和不幸的摄取，互联网都再度让这些东西倍增。特别是最后一项，伦理和良知的——世界很不好，我都能看见，但我又终归帮不了。过度沉湎其中，我也无法正常生活。那么一种更深度的倦怠是难免的。
content.en:
This article was published in November 2023 on the Dunes Workshop WeChat Official Account—
Years ago, during my first trip to Tokyo, I was struck by the city's sheer density. It wasn’t just the density of buildings and population, but a holistic "urban density"—where everything is packed to the absolute brim. Countless graphics and multilingual texts seem desperate to slap you right across the eyes. Back then, I lacked the reflections on capitalism and the "society of the spectacle"; I was simply held fast by the gravity of the metropolis, feeling as though I wanted to see and notice every single thing.
When I spoke with a classmate who had lived in Japan for a long time, her immediate reaction was: "That feeling will pass." Looking back, that is exactly what Georg Simmel called the #blasé attitude#. It is impossible for someone to live in Tokyo for ten years and still be wide-eyed at those streets every time they step out. "Blasé" becomes an almost inevitable mental defense mechanism, preventing the brain from overloading under excessive stimulation.
Inside a Pachinko parlor, the clatter of silver balls is deafening. Rows of customers pull levers repeatedly while screen animations flash frantically, one sound effect drowning out the next. Stepping in for the first time, your ears and eyes simply can’t cope. My classmate turned and said, "After a while, you’ll find this actually relieves stress." It seems the "blasé" shell of the Japanese #salaryman# is indeed much thicker than mine; their "tolerance" has built up to the point where they require this level of dosage. Strangely, though, I’ve started to understand it over the past year—the TV is on in the living room while I scroll through social media in my room, perhaps even with a podcast playing simultaneously. Oddly, that state of being saturated by media actually allows one to "space out" for a short while. John Mulaney described his state in New York in a stand-up set: "I've been in a fugue state since 2014... walking into traffic like Charlie Chaplin, listening to a podcast in my ears and thinking about another podcast in my head." On one hand, becoming indifferent to all kinds of sensory stimuli; on the other, being immersed in them and unwilling to leave, needing an "overdose" during leisure time just to feel comfortable—this is the mental condition of the urbanite.
Blaséness also points to the thick shell one gradually cultivates in social conduct. Compared to the "society of acquaintances" in rural areas, people living in cities encounter dozens or hundreds of times more strangers and engage in interactions ranging from the superficial to the profound. Knowing that some relationships are inevitably fleeting, that some people harbor ill intentions, or have diametrically opposed interests, the social mode developed by the "urbanite" naturally shifts toward sophistication, indifference, or detachment. Giving your heart to everyone you meet in a metropolis is both inefficient and leaves you vulnerable to hurt.
Finally, I want to extend this interpersonal aspect to a kind of ethical or conscientious blaséness. Louis C.K., poking fun at New Yorkers' attitudes toward the homeless, said: "There's too many homeless people, you have to make a choice. You can't help all of them. And so, of course, you help none of them." I prefer another of his bits. He talks about a friend in New York who had a cousin visiting from a small town. This was the cousin's first time in the big city, and she was clearly nowhere near used to the sight of homeless people everywhere. Just as they picked her up from the station and started walking out, the girl saw a homeless man in a corner, covered in trash and reeking. Horrified, she rushed forward, knelt on one knee, and asked anxiously, "Sir, what’s wrong? What happened?" At that moment, Louis and his friend rushed over, grabbed this "naive country girl," and said, "No, no, no—we don’t do that here!"
This "correction" is, of course, absurd, but it is highly telling. In a metropolis where filthy people, events, and things gather like a swirling vortex, long-term residents have trained a character of numbness—the ability to look without seeing. If a New Yorker were to pay attention to and inquire about every crime, injustice, and misfortune occurring in the city, they wouldn't be able to live their own lives at all. It has almost become a code of conduct for survival here. Thus, the two rushed forward to stop the cousin who wanted to help, like a host teaching a guest table manners: "We don’t do that here!" This, too, is a form of being blasé.
It must be mentioned that if the emergence of the modern metropolis at the end of the 19th century allowed the sociologist Simmel to observe the appearance of new people, new characters, and a new spirit, then for us today, social media is an equivalent—or even more extreme—condition. Whether it is the quantity of images, the intensity of stimulation, the number of interpersonal contacts, or the consumption of suffering and misfortune, the Internet has once again multiplied these factors. Especially the last one—the ethical and conscientious: the world is in bad shape, I can see it all, but ultimately, I cannot help. If I indulge in it too much, I cannot live a normal life. Thus, a deeper level of blaséness is inevitable.

brief_definition.zh: 拥有唯一性的作品所产生的距离感，权威性和本真性
brief_definition.en: The phenomenon of distance [Erscheinung einer Ferne], authority, and authenticity generated by a work of unique existence.

zh: 想象在一个夏日的午后，你躺在草地上，目光追随着远处连绵山脉的轮廓。在那一刻，你感受到了那座山独特的“呼吸”。这是一种不可复制的、此时此地的独特体验。然而，当你拿起手机拍下那座山时，那种微妙的震颤便消失了。
在《机械复制时代的艺术作品》一文中，本雅明敏锐地捕捉到，即使是最完美的复制品也总是缺少一样东西，那就是艺术品在时间和空间中独一无二的存在。本雅明在文中列举了青铜器、中世纪手稿以及夏日午后远山的轮廓来阐释“灵韵”——那是一种无论距离多近，仍保有距离感的独特现象。由于艺术品最初的仪式功能，它们似乎带有源自另一个世界的神圣光彩。
在机械复制时代，大众愈发渴望将事物“拉近”。现代技术（如摄影和电影）通过批量生产，将艺术品从神庙和博物馆的“神坛”上拉了下来，送到了大众手中。大众可以通过占有摹本或复制品来占有事物本身。复制品的暂时性和可重复性取代了艺术品的独特性和永久性，从而摧毁了它的“灵韵”。
对本雅明而言，本真的艺术品起源于仪式，而“灵韵”也无法脱离仪式性。因此，“灵韵”的消逝同时也让艺术从传统仪式的根基中解放了出来。
en: Imagine lying on the grass on a summer afternoon, your gaze following the contours of a distant mountain range. At that moment, you feel the mountain's unique "breath." However, the moment you pick up your phone to capture the mountain, that subtle tremor vanishes.

In The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction, Walter Benjamin astutely observes that even the most perfect reproduction lacks one element of the original artwork: its unique presence in time and space. Benjamin cites examples such as bronze statues, medieval manuscripts, and the contours of a distant mountain on a summer afternoon to illustrate the "Aura"—defined as the unique phenomenon of a distance, however close it may be. Rooted in their original ritualistic function, works of art seem to possess a sacred radiance, almost as if from another world.

In the age of mechanical reproduction, the masses increasingly yearn to bring things "closer." Modern technologies (such as photography and film) have pulled artworks down from the "altars" of temples and museums, placing them into the hands of the masses. The public can possess the object itself by possessing a copy or reproduction. The transience and reproducibility of the copy replace the authenticity and permanence of the original artwork, thereby shattering its "Aura."
For Benjamin, the absence of the "Aura" in the age of mechanical reproduction simultaneously emancipates art from the foundations of traditional ritual.

example_sentence.zh: 工业生产和机械复制让艺术品不再具有从前的独有性，那么人工智能技术的生成式创造，是否更进一步使得事物的“灵韵”消逝了？
example_sentence.en: If industrial production and mechanical reproduction deprived works of art of their former uniqueness, does the generative creation of artificial intelligence further accelerate the withering of the "Aura"?

content.zh: 或许影像媒介本身就更擅长制造一种易于被“消费”的“美学”？
content.en: Perhaps the medium of the image is inherently better at manufacturing an "aesthetic" that is easily "consumed"?

content.zh:
对于本雅明而言，灵韵的消逝带着一种辩证的希望。“机械复制时代”打破了精英对艺术的垄断，让艺术走向了政治。
桑塔格则更为悲观，在《论摄影》中，武装了照相机的窥视者（Voyeur）拒绝尊重这种距离。相机“捕捉”并“占有”了被摄主体，将私人领域公开化、将遥远之物拉近。一旦你拍摄了某物，你就已经消费了它，使其成为收藏品的一部分，而不再是一个鲜活的、有生命力的实体。
摄影技术将美国变成一个消费的景观，桑塔格的“窥视者”（或者说摄影师）是更极致的消费主义世界中的“游荡者”（Flâneur）。对于本雅明而言，游荡者仍然在人群中寻找独特的体验，带有“距离感”的灵韵，虽然它已经变得难以寻觅。然而另一方面，这种漫游的行为本身也已经商业化了，游荡者自身的“光晕”也随之消逝。
最近重温一些电影和摄影集时，我发现影像总能赋予那些极其普通的城市空间一种“美感”。无论是Stephen Shore镜头下的美国郊区，贾樟柯电影里的中国乡村，还是Wolfgang Tillmans记录的日常生活，都呈现出一种超越了建筑空间本身的独特质感。它们似乎成功地构建了一种与“现实”的“距离感”，从而使图像具备了一种“乡愁”。这种效果在其他媒介中似乎难以复刻，或许影像媒介本身就更擅长制造一种易于被“消费”的“美学”？
content.en:
For Benjamin, the decay of aura carries a spark of dialectical hope. The "age of mechanical reproduction" shattered the elite monopoly on art, steering it toward the realm of politics.
Sontag, however, was far more pessimistic. In #On Photography#, armed with camera, the voyeur refuses to respect such distance. The camera "captures" and "possesses" the subject, making the private public and bringing the remote within reach. Once you photograph something, you have consumed it, turning it into a mere collectible rather than a living, breathing entity.
Photographic technology has transformed America into a landscape of consumption; Sontag’s "voyeur" (or photographer) is a more extreme version of the #flâneur# in a consumerist world. For Benjamin, the #flâneur# still seeks unique experiences within the crowd—an aura of "distance," however elusive it has become. Yet, on the other hand, the act of wandering itself has become commodified, and the #flâneur#’s own "halo" has vanished along with it.
Revisiting some films and photography books, I’ve noticed how images consistently imbue mundane urban spaces with "aesthetic beauty." Whether it’s the American suburbs through the lens of Stephen Shore, the Chinese countryside in #Jia Zhangke#'s films, or the everyday life documented by Wolfgang Tillmans, they all present a unique texture that transcends the physical space. They seem to successfully construct a "sense of distance" from "reality," thereby endowing the images with a form of "nostalgia." This effect seems difficult to replicate in other media. Perhaps the medium of the image is inherently better at manufacturing an "aesthetic" that is easily "consumed"?

brief_definition.zh: 作品内部嵌套的、对作品整体进行微缩映射的递归结构
brief_definition.en: A recursive structure embedded within a work that serves as a miniature reflection of the whole.

zh: 想象站在两面平行的镜子之间，两面镜子互相反射，镜中的画面不断复制，形成深不可测的空间。“Mise en abîme”一词常被用于描述这种视觉体验。
“Mise en abîme”的字面意思为“陷入深渊”或“放置在深渊中”。最初，在纹章学术语中，“abyme”指盾形纹章的中心，因此，“Mise en abîme”意为“放在中心”，即在大的盾形纹章中间镶嵌一个小的盾形纹章。
后来法国作家安德烈·纪德将其应用于现代批评中，被译为“叙事内镜”，用以阐释一种特殊的艺术结构：在作品（如小说、绘画、电影等）内部嵌入一个微缩的、与整体相似的“复制品”。这个“内部的小作品”会以某种方式反映、概括、预示或评论整个大作品的主题、结构或情节。最经典的例子是《哈姆雷特》中的“捕鼠机”一幕：哈姆雷特安排了一场戏中戏，戏的内容恰恰是谋杀国王——这出小戏像一面镜子，照出了整部大戏的核心真相。
叙事内镜打破了作品的封闭性，它像一面镜子，让作品开始“自我反思”。这种精巧的结构游戏引导读者或观众去思考“现实”与“虚构”的边界。当你意识到你所看的故事，正在被故事里的人重演或观看时，你便会和作者一同进入一个关于“讲述”本身的奇妙迷宫。
en: Imagine standing between two parallel mirrors reflecting each other, creating an infinite regression of images that forms an unfathomable depth. The term "Mise en abîme" is often used to describe this visual experience.

Literally meaning "placed into the abyss," the term originates from heraldry. In this context, the "abîme" referred to the center of a coat of arms. Thus, "Mise en abîme" described the practice of embedding a smaller shield within the center of a larger one.

Later, French writer André Gide appropriated the term for modern criticism to describe a specific artistic structure: the embedding of a miniature "replica" within a work (such as a novel, painting, or film) that bears a resemblance to the whole. This "internal work" reflects, summarizes, foreshadows, or comments on the themes, structure, or plot of the overarching work. A classic example is the "Mousetrap" scene in Hamlet. Hamlet orchestrates a play-within-a-play that depicts the murder of a king; this inner play acts as a mirror, reflecting the core truth of the larger drama.

This recursive structure shatters the enclosed nature of a work of art, inviting the reader or viewer to contemplate the boundaries between "reality" and "fiction." When the story is being reenacted by characters within the story itself, the audience enters a labyrinth regarding the act of storytelling.

example_sentence.zh: 这部小说构建了一个令人眩晕的叙事内镜：主人公在布满灰尘的旧书架上发现了一份手稿，而手稿里详细讲述的故事，恰恰就是此刻他发现这份手稿的过程。
example_sentence.en: The novel constructs a dizzying mise en abîme: the protagonist discovers a manuscript on a dusty old shelf, only to find that the story narrated within details the very moment of him finding the manuscript.

content.zh: 对我来说Mise en abyme的结构就像是这样的环形，或者是一条被反复描画过无数次的线条，周围有钢笔反复的痕迹，但是很难找到最初的是哪条。
content.en: To me, the structure of #mise en abyme# is like this kind of circle—or perhaps a single line that has been traced over countless times. You can see the overlapping marks of the pen where it has repeatedly swept across the page, yet it is nearly impossible to find which stroke was the original.

content.zh:
当我们把两面镜子相对放置在一起，两边产生好似永无止境的镜中镜画面，像两条没有终点的隧道，或者永不见底的深渊。不难理解为什么部分中文翻译有时也会用“镜渊”一词来指代Mise en abyme。埃舍尔的作品《画廊》（Print Gallery）就是这样一幅看上去没有终点的画作，通过图像的放大、迭代与拆分，形成无限重复的效果。无论从哪个点开始观看，视线最后都会被引回起点。在叙事内镜的结构中，真实和虚构往往会模糊不清，难以分辨。

以博尔赫斯《环形废墟》（The Circular Ruins）为例，魔法师逃到一座被火焚毁的火神庙想要实现他的意志，即创造一个世界上不曾有过的人。他在梦中塑造了这个“儿子”的心脏、肉身与意识，并最终将其带入现实世界。唯有“火”本身和魔法师知道他是个幻影，证据是不会被火烧伤。在一次意外中火神庙再次焚于大火中，而魔法师却发现自己也不过只是另一人梦中的幻影。
这总是让我联想到佛教中的因果轮回观。今世如果是前世的业报，那么现世将是无穷尽的，好似没有源头。而在“叙事内镜”的结构中，故事和故事相互嵌套，真实渐隐于不断的映照中，没有哪一层是绝对的意义源头。《红楼梦》中对金陵十二钗的判词、戏文、诗词，同样预示着书中角色的生命走向，每个人的命运都在大观园的大兴衰中交织出因果的网，且“假作真时真亦假”。无论是前世绛珠仙草今世林黛玉，无论是木石前盟还是金玉良缘，情与欲、生与死，前世与今世等看上去二元的概念在书中界限往往都模糊而层层叠叠，而并非泾渭分明。

阿伦·雷乃的电影《去年在马里昂巴德》（Last Year at Marienbad）则以更为抽象的方式呈现了 mise en abyme 的结构。影片中的人物不断复述、修正同一段“记忆”，叙述本身被不断重复和修改，而记忆也在反复的讲述中变得模糊，以至于像一个不断重复的环形结构。

对我来说Mise en abyme的结构就像是这样的环形，或者是一条被反复描画过无数次的线条，周围有钢笔反复的痕迹，但是很难找到最初的是哪条。
content.en:
When we place two mirrors directly opposite each other, they produce an apparently endless image-within-an-image, like two tunnels without an exit or a bottomless abyss. It is easy to see why some Chinese translations use the term #Mirror Abyss# (#镜渊#) to refer to #Mise en abyme#. M.C. Escher’s work #Print Gallery# is precisely this kind of "endless" artwork; through the magnification, iteration, and fragmentation of the image, it creates an effect of infinite repetition. No matter where the viewer's eye begins, it is eventually led back to the starting point. Within the structure of this "narrative inner mirror," the boundaries between reality and fiction often become blurred and indistinguishable.

Taking Borges’ #The Circular Ruins# as an example, a magician retreats to a fire-gutted temple of the God of Fire, intent on exerting his will: to dream a man into being—a man who never existed in this world. In his dreams, he molds the "son’s" heart, flesh, and consciousness, eventually leading him into the physical realm. Only Fire itself and the magician know that the son is a phantom, proven by his immunity to flames. During an accident, the temple is once again consumed by fire, only for the magician to discover that he, too, is merely a phantom in another man’s dream.

This always brings to mind the Buddhist concept of #Samsara# and karmic retribution. If this life is the karmic fruit of a previous one, then existence becomes an inexhaustible cycle, as if having no origin. Within the structure of "narrative recursion," stories are nested within stories; reality gradually fades amidst constant reflections, and no single layer serves as the absolute source of meaning. Similarly, in #Dream of the Red Chamber#, the prophecies for the "Twelve Beauties of Jinling," the opera plays, and the poetry all foreshadow the life paths of the characters. Each destiny is interwoven into a web of cause and effect within the rise and fall of Prospect Garden, where #truth becomes fiction when the fiction's true#. Whether it is the reincarnation of the Crimson Pearl Herb as Lin Daiyu, or the "Alliance of Wood and Stone" versus the "Predestined Marriage of Gold and Jade," binary concepts like love and lust, life and death, and past and present lives are often blurred and layered rather than clearly demarcated.

Alain Resnais’ film #Last Year at Marienbad# presents the #mise en abyme# structure in an even more abstract fashion. The characters in the film constantly recount and revise the same "memory"; the narration itself is repeatedly looped and modified until the memory becomes so blurred in the retelling that it resembles an endlessly repeating circular structure.

To me, the structure of #mise en abyme# is like this kind of circle—or perhaps a single line that has been traced over countless times. You can see the overlapping marks of the pen where it has repeatedly swept across the page, yet it is nearly impossible to find which stroke was the original.

brief_definition.zh: 一种对记忆进行记录与保存的强烈欲望，以及与之共生的、潜在于归档行为中的对记忆的破坏与摧毁
brief_definition.en: A compulsive desire to record and preserve memory, with the inherent, latent destruction of that memory

zh: 1994年，在伦敦弗洛伊德博物馆——这位心理学大师生前的最后居所——雅克·德里达发表了关于“档案”的主题演讲。对德里达而言，这一场所深刻地影响了对“档案”的探讨：弗洛伊德的精神分析记录、档案，以及这一居所向“博物馆”的身份转型，都为讨论增添了多重维度。他敏锐地察觉到，“档案”与“精神分析”之间存在着复杂的联系，这种联系反映在私人与公共程序、制度、学术乃至法律的档案化过程之中。
在包括弗洛伊德在内的人类身上，德里达诊断出一种关于档案的“热病”（Archive Fever）。这是一种“强迫性的、重复且怀旧的欲望，表现为一种抑制不住的、试图回归源头的渴望；一种指向最古老、最绝对的发端场所的乡愁。”在当下，我们那些存满了聊天记录与生活碎片、容量庞大的云端硬盘，亦可被视为这种“热病”的表征。

德里达将这种“热病”与弗洛伊德提出的“死亡冲动”联系起来。正是由于对遗忘的恐惧，我们才建立档案，试图以此追寻那“绝对的起点”。然而，档案并非记忆本身，而仅是记忆的辅助器材，一种“义肢”（prosthetic）。它将原本“自然”且“内在”的记忆，寄存在可被阅读、复制的外部媒介（如纸张或硬盘）之上。因此，档案本身即是一个充满矛盾的概念：建立档案的前提恰恰是原生记忆的丧失与毁灭。可以说，档案在先验层面便是反对自身的。
在德里达看来，精神分析所构建的心理档案本质上也是一种“制度”与“建制”，标志着人类与自然状态的彻底决裂。由此，精神分析理论不仅是关于心理与记忆的学说，更演变成为一种关于档案的理论。
有趣的是，对德里达来说，档案并不只是关于“过去”的研究，更能影响未来。因为“归档行为”本身就在生产事件：档案的“技术底色”（technical substrate）预先决定了什么是“可被归档的”，进而反过来塑造了我们的生活经验。正如当下的短视频已经预设了特定的时长、画幅、记录逻辑与交互方式，这在很大程度上决定了未来的历史将以何种面貌呈现。
en: In 1994, at the Freud Museum in London—the psychoanalyst’s final residence—Jacques Derrida delivered a lecture on the "archive." For Derrida, this setting was more than a venue; it profoundly shaped his inquiry. Freud’s records and the transition of his home from a private residence to a museum added layers of meaning to the discussion. Derrida recognized a complex link between the archive and psychoanalysis, one that ripples through private and public programs and institutionalized process.

Derrida diagnosed a condition he called "Archive Fever" (Mal d'Archive) in many figures, including Freud. He described it as "a compulsive, repetitive, and nostalgic desire to return to the origin." Today, we see this "fever" manifest in our massive cloud drives, which overflow with years of chat logs, photos, apps, and other fragments of our lives.

Derrida linked this fever to Freud’s "death drive." The fear of forgetting compels us to build archives in the hope of recording a "starting point." Yet, the archive is not memory (mnēmē) itself; it is a prosthesis—a "hypomnesic" memory. It takes what was once "natural" and "internal" and consigns it to external, reproducible media like paper or hard drives. The archive is paradoxical: the very condition for its existence is the loss or destruction of the original, living memory. In this sense, the archive is "a priori, against itself."

For Derrida, psychoanalysis is itself a form of institutional archiving—a decisive break from a state of natural memory toward an external record of events. Consequently, psychoanalysis is not merely a study of the mind and memory; it becomes a theory of the archive itself.

example_sentence.zh: 每一顿饭他都拍照记录，这种档案热让他拥有了完美的数字记录，却也让他发现，如果没有手机里的照片，他甚至无法记起昨晚食物的味道。
example_sentence.en: He photographed every dish he had. While this archive fever left him with a perfect digital record, he eventually realized that without those photos, he couldn't even recall the taste of last night's dinner.

caption.en: Freud's library at the Freud Museum London

content.zh: 斯底德曼认为，“档案热”不仅是一种隐喻，也是一种真实的职业病，源于著名史学家儒勒·米什莱（Jules Michelet）由于多年在档案馆工作，吸入过多尘埃和病菌所导致的疾病。
content.en: Steedman argues that "archive fever" is not merely a metaphor but a genuine occupational disease, exemplified by the famous historian Jules Michelet, who fell ill after years of inhaling the dust and pathogens of the archives.

content.zh: 历史学家卡罗琳·斯底德曼（Carolyn Steedman）不完全认同德里达对“档案”的隐喻化解读，同时她提出了一种更为具体的“物质性”可能性。斯底德曼认为，“档案热”不仅是一种隐喻，也是一种真实的职业病，源于著名史学家儒勒·米什莱（Jules Michelet）由于多年在档案馆工作，吸入过多尘埃和病菌所导致的疾病。疾病源于“尘埃的物质存在，这些尘埃是动物躯体经历艰辛与磨难、成长与衰亡后残存的原子残骸。”这些尘埃在档案室中通过历史学家的研究和处理转变为其他形态，但从未真正消失。
content.en: Historian Carolyn Steedman does not fully subscribe to Derrida’s metaphorical reading of the "archive," proposing instead a possibility grounded in a more concrete "materiality." Steedman argues that "archive fever" is not merely a metaphor but a genuine occupational disease, exemplified by the famous historian Jules Michelet, who fell ill after years of inhaling the dust and pathogens of the archives. This malady stems from "the physical existence of dust, which is the atomic remains of animal bodies, their pain and their endurance, their growth and their decay." Through the historian’s research and handling, this dust is transmuted into other forms within the archive, yet it never truly vanishes.

content.zh:
有趣的是，对德里达来说，档案并不只是关于“过去”的研究，更能影响未来。因为“归档行为”本身就在生产事件：档案的“技术底色”（technical substrate）预先决定了什么是“可被归档的”，进而反过来塑造了我们的生活经验。正如当下的短视频已经预设了特定的时长、画幅、记录逻辑与交互方式，这在很大程度上决定了未来的历史将以何种面貌呈现。
虽然德里达所讲的“技术底色”更关注一种概念层面上“媒介”的影响，但斯底德曼提到的物质层面的“灰尘和病菌”其实也是“技术底色”中重要的一环，在数字时代，档案的这种物质性（或者说对于身体的影响）消失了吗？还是说，数字档案对身体的“改造”反而变得更加隐蔽且剧烈了？
从更大于身体的尺度上去思考，在建筑与空间上，这种物质性的影响似乎变得更加直接和粗暴了，过去的档案存在于“档案馆”或“博物馆”这样具体的、可以进入、可以有空间体验的场所；而现在的档案则依赖于“数据中心”这些与我们具身的空间体验剥离的场所。
在档案的使用者看来，物质性的消失，但实际上数据中心与物质世界的交互是更“原始”的、能源的消耗。如果德里达将“档案”描述为一种“外部性”（将生动的记忆转化为一种外接的“义肢”），那么“数据中心”就像传统的“档案馆”的“义肢”，一种更彻底的“外部”。SpaceX 的 Starlink（星链） 正在太空中构建一个庞大的数据传输网络，这或许构成了最极致的“外部化”。
content.en:
Derrida argued that archiving is not just about the past—it dictates the future. The act of archiving actually produces the event as much as it records it. The "technical substrate" (the medium we use) predetermines what is "archivable," which in turn shapes our actual lived experience. Just as "reels" pre-determined the duration, framing, and modes of interaction for our lives, the technology of the archive decides what our  history will be.
While Derrida’s concept of the "technical substrate" focuses primarily on the conceptual impact of the medium, Steedman’s emphasis on the material reality—the "dust and pathogens"—is actually an indispensable element of this substrate. In the digital age, has this materiality of the archive, its direct impact on the body, vanished? Or has the digital archive "reconfigured" the body in a more insidious and profound way?
When we move beyond the scale of the body to the architecture and urban scale, this material impact appears, paradoxically, even more direct and brutal. Historical, "archives" and "museums" are physically accessible sites with an embodied spatial experience. However, "data centers" are severed from our physical presence and sensory experience.
To the digital archival user, materiality seems to have evaporated. Yet, in reality, the data center’s interaction with the physical world is far more "primitive," the raw consumption of energy. If Derrida defines the "archive" as a form of "exteriority"—the transfer of living memory into an external "prosthesis"—then the data center functions as the prosthesis of the traditional archive itself, a more radical "exterior." Consider SpaceX’s Starlink, which is currently constructing a massive data transmission network in space; this perhaps constitutes the ultimate form of "exteriorization."

brief_definition.zh: 提倡关注文本表面含义的诠释方法
brief_definition.en: An interpretive method that advocates for focusing on the literal meaning of the text

zh: 当你翻开一本诗集，不再绞尽脑汁地猜测诗人是否在隐喻社会不公或心理创伤，而是单纯地沉醉于文字的韵律、纸张的触感，以及诗句中描绘的蓝天白云，你可能正在接近“表层阅读”的核心：它鼓励我们放下“侦探”般的猜疑，回归文本的可见表面。

表层阅读源于对传统文学批评方法的反思。在20世纪，主流批评如“症候阅读”（Symptomatic Reading）或“妄想阅读”（Paranoid Reading）要求读者扮演多疑的侦探，坚信文本背后隐藏着深层含义、意识形态或“症状”，必须挖掘出来才能揭示真相。例如，在分析一部小说时，批评家可能会过度解读一个角色的行为，将其视为资本主义压迫的象征。然而，表层阅读反对这种“深度挖掘”，转而强调文本的表面元素：包括语言的结构、字面意义、物质形式（如书籍的物理属性），以及显而易见的规律。它倡导一种“不带有妄想和猜忌”的阅读态度，旨在让读者从过度解读的负担中解放出来，在文学本身的享受中获得自由——就像在公园里，你不再为每片落叶赋予象征意义，而是单纯欣赏它的飘落之美。 这种方法并非否定深度，而是提醒我们：文本的表面同样丰富。它有助于避免主观臆断，促进更客观的文学分析，同时让阅读回归愉悦的本质。在数字时代，表层阅读还呼应了人们对信息过载的反思，鼓励我们慢下来，专注于眼前的内容。
en: When you open a collection of poems and no longer rack your brain wondering if the poet is using a metaphor for social injustice or psychological trauma, but instead simply lose yourself in the rhythm of the words, the texture of the paper, and the blue skies and white clouds depicted in the verses, you are perhaps approaching the core of surface reading. It encourages us to lay down our "detective-like" suspicions and return to the visible surface of the text.

Surface reading stems from a reflection on traditional methods of literary criticism. In the 20th century, mainstream critiques such as "symptomatic reading" or "paranoid reading" required readers to act as suspicious detectives, convinced that deep meanings, ideologies, or "symptoms" were hidden behind the text and had to be excavated to reveal the truth. For instance, when analyzing a novel, a critic might over-interpret a character’s behavior, viewing it as a symbol of capitalist oppression. However, surface reading opposes this "deep excavation," emphasizing instead the surface elements of the text: its linguistic structure, literal meaning, material form (such as the physical attributes of the book), and its obvious patterns. It advocates for a reading attitude "devoid of paranoia and suspicion," aiming to liberate readers from the burden of over-interpretation and find freedom in the enjoyment of literature itself—much like being in a park where you no longer assign symbolic meaning to every falling leaf, but simply admire the beauty of its descent.

This method does not deny depth; rather, it reminds us that the surface of a text is equally rich. It helps avoid subjective speculation, fosters more objective literary analysis, and allows reading to return to its essence of pleasure. In the digital age, surface reading also echoes reflections on information overload, encouraging us to slow down and focus on what is right before our eyes.

example_sentence.zh: 在讨论一部现代小说时，教授建议学生采用表层阅读的方法，专注于分析对话的节奏和场景描述的视觉细节，而不是急于推断作者的潜在政治立场。
example_sentence.en: When discussing a contemporary novel, the professor encouraged students to adopt Surface Reading, focusing on analyzing the cadence of dialogue and visual details of scene descriptions rather than hastily inferring the author’s latent political stance.

content.zh: 我比较担心的是“表层阅读”像是一种情绪上的反弹：我累了，不想再当侦探了。我觉得这很真实，也很必要。但如果把它当成唯一正确的方法，那可能又走到了另一个极端。
content.en: My concern is that "superficial reading" is more of an emotional reaction: "I'm tired, I don't want to be a detective anymore." I think this is realistic and necessary. But if it's considered the only correct method, then it might swing to the other extreme.

content.zh: 我好奇的是表层阅读是否也有一套比较严格的方法——类似于“暂停怀疑”（suspension of skepticism)的阅读方法。事实上，究竟如何阅读应当是一个比较矛盾的过程，既有“不求甚解”也有“追根究底”可能才是最好的，我比较担心的是“表层阅读”像是一种情绪上的反弹：我累了，不想再当侦探了。我觉得这很真实，也很必要。但如果把它当成唯一正确的方法，那可能又走到了另一个极端。确实，过度的“分析解读”内在是一种控制欲，总想控制、揭露、占有意义，把文学当成了战斗对象。“表层阅读”强调回到语言本身、回到显现出来的样子，这在某种程度上是更“此在式”的，是一种愿意停下来、愿意被打动的阅读，这个态度值得学习，但象征、隐喻、深层意义恰恰是很多经典文本的生命力所在。
content.en: I'm curious whether superficial reading also has a relatively rigorous method—similar to the "suspension of disbelief" approach to reading.  In fact, how one should read is likely a rather contradictory process; a combination of "not seeking complete understanding" and "pursuing thorough investigation" might be best. My concern is that "superficial reading" is more of an emotional reaction: "I'm tired, I don't want to be a detective anymore." I think this is realistic and necessary. But if it's considered the only correct method, then it might swing to the other extreme. Indeed, Excessive "analysis and interpretation" is inherently a form of control, a desire to control, expose, and possess meaning, treating literature as an object of conquest. "Surface reading" emphasizes returning to language itself, to what is immediately apparent, which is in a sense more "existential," a reading attitude that is willing to pause and be moved. This attitude is worth learning, but symbolism, metaphor, and deeper meanings are precisely what give many classic texts their vitality.

brief_definition.zh: 对他人的关怀行为经常因为不被视作“正式劳动”而被忽视的劳动者群体
brief_definition.en: A group of laborers whose acts of care for others are frequently overlooked because they are not recognized as "formal labor"

zh: 一名护士刚结束夜班，她不仅完成了输液、记录体征等“分内事”，更在一位焦虑的癌症患者床边多停留了半小时，握着他的手，听他倾诉对治疗的恐惧和家庭的担忧。这份工作记录表上无法量化、绩效考核难以体现的付出，这正是“关怀阶级”劳动的缩影。
下层劳动者大量的工作是关心他人，而非机械的流水线生产。如，检票员大部分时间不在检票，而是指路、维护设施、寻找走丢的小孩、照顾老人、病人等。大量女性承担的家务牵扯情感、时间、精力，但并不在传统的“劳动”框架中。这样的关怀可能并不生产实际的“商品”或“有用之物”，却为商品的生产以及正式的劳动能够运行提供了基础。
关注“关怀阶层”，有助于突显更多人的劳动，以及大量被忽视的劳动时间和内容。与此同时，“关怀”与官僚和行政管理形成对比，后者更关注工作的标准化，而前者非标准化的工作落脚点在他人如何获益。关注“关怀”有助于摆脱以生产、消费、标准化效率为核心的经济模式，转向一种有益于人的实际互助福祉的公共经济。
en: A nurse has just finished her night shift. She didn't just complete her "official duties"—administering IVs and recording vitals—but spent an extra half-hour by the bed of an anxious cancer patient, holding his hand and listening to his fears about treatment and worries for his family. This effort, unquantifiable on a work log and invisible to performance appraisals, is the epitome of labor within the "caring class."

A vast amount of work performed by lower-tier laborers involves caring for others rather than mechanical assembly-line production. For instance, ticket inspectors spend most of their time not checking tickets, but giving directions, maintaining facilities, finding lost children, and assisting the elderly or the sick. Similarly, the domestic labor performed by a large number of women involves emotions, time, and energy, yet it does not fit into the traditional framework of "labor." Such care may not produce actual "commodities" or "useful objects," yet it provides the very foundation upon which commodity production and formal labor are able to function.

Focusing on the "caring class" helps highlight the labor of more people, as well as the vast amounts of overlooked labor time and content. Meanwhile, "care" stands in contrast to bureaucracy and administration; the latter prioritizes the standardization of work, while the former’s non-standardized efforts are rooted in how others benefit. Prioritizing "care" helps us break away from an economic model centered on production, consumption, and standardized efficiency, shifting instead toward a public economy beneficial to actual mutual aid and human well-being.

example_sentence.zh: 部分批判性社会理论忽视"关怀", 认为"关怀"是私人，家庭领域的活动，缺乏政治性讨论的可能，是对积极行动和结构性变革的逃避，有去政治化的色彩。然而很多时候，"关怀阶级"营造了公共空间和公共变革的前提，也应当被重新思考。
example_sentence.en: Some critical social theories overlook "care", considering it an activity within the private and family domains, lacking the possibility of political discussion, and seeing it as an evasion of active action and structural change, with a depoliticizing tint. However, many times, the "care class" has created the preconditions for public space and public change and should be rethought.

content.zh: 这样的关怀可能并不生产实际的“商品”或“有用之物”，却为商品的生产以及正式的劳动能够运行提供了基础。
content.en: Such care may not produce tangible "commodities" or "useful objects," yet it provides the very foundation upon which the production of goods and formal labor can function.

content.zh:
下层劳动者大量的工作是关心他人，而非机械的流水线生产。如，检票员大部分时间不在检票，而是指路、维护设施、寻找走丢的小孩、照顾老人、病人等。大量女性承担的家务牵扯情感、时间、精力，但并不在传统的“劳动”框架中。这样的关怀可能并不生产实际的“商品”或“有用之物”，却为商品的生产以及正式的劳动能够运行提供了基础。
        
关注“关怀阶层”，有助于突显更多人的劳动，以及大量被忽视的劳动时间和内容。与此同时，“关怀”与官僚和行政管理形成对比，后者更关注工作的标准化，而前者非标准化的工作落脚点在他人如何获益。关注“关怀”有助于摆脱以生产、消费、标准化效率为核心的经济模式，转向一种有益于人的实际互助福祉的公共经济。
content.en:
A significant portion of the work performed by lower-class laborers consists of caring for others rather than mechanical assembly-line production. For instance, a ticket inspector spends the majority of their time not punching tickets, but giving directions, maintaining facilities, finding lost children, and tending to the elderly or the sick. Similarly, the vast amount of housework undertaken by women involves a deep investment of emotion, time, and energy, yet it remains outside the traditional framework of "labor." Such care may not produce tangible "commodities" or "useful objects," yet it provides the very foundation upon which the production of goods and formal labor can function.
Focusing on the "caring class" helps highlight the labor of a broader population, as well as the vast amount of overlooked working hours and tasks. At the same time, "care" stands in stark contrast to bureaucracy and administration; while the latter focuses on the standardization of work, the former consists of non-standardized tasks centered on how others benefit. Prioritizing "care" helps us break away from an economic model centered on production, consumption, and standardized efficiency, shifting instead toward a public economy that fosters actual mutual aid and human well-being.

brief_definition.zh: 现代化进程过快导致的高度压缩时空共存状况
brief_definition.en: A condition of highly compressed spatiotemporal coexistence resulting from excessively rapid modernization processes.

zh: 在一款模拟建造的游戏中，你需要在短短几年内将一个小村庄发展成高科技大都市。你疯狂地建造工厂、摩天大楼和AI数据中心，但村庄里的老庙宇还没拆除，居民们一边用智能手机点外卖，一边参加传统祭祀活动，同时担心机器人会抢走他们的工作。这种混乱而快速的转型，就是压缩现代性的缩影——不同时代元素被硬生生挤进同一个时空里。
压缩现代性描述的是社会变迁中时间和空间被极度压缩的现象。当现代化进程过快时，前现代（如传统农业社会）、现代（如工业化城市）和后现代（如数字风险和全球化）元素被迫共存，形成一种流动而复合的体系。
以韩国为例，它在20世纪后半叶仅用50年就完成了西方200-300年的工业化和经济增长，导致社会同时呈现发达国家的高科技、不发达国家的贫困问题以及独特的文化冲突。例如，首尔的年轻人可能一边追求个人主义（后现代），一边被家庭责任（前现代）束缚，同时面临经济不稳定（现代风险）。这种压缩性催生了“快文化”——结果主义、指标至上和效率优先，但也带来复合风险，如环境危机或社会分裂。
张庆燮将这一概念扩展到东亚，中国改革开放的快速转型也类似：传统家庭价值观与现代个体主义交织，阎云翔等学者用它分析中国社会变迁。本质上，压缩现代性揭示了快速发展的代价：历史被折叠，社会在矛盾中前行。
en: In a city-building simulation game, you are tasked with transforming a small village into a high-tech metropolis within a mere few years. You frantically construct factories, skyscrapers, and AI data centers, yet the village's ancient temples remain standing. Residents order takeout via smartphones while participating in traditional sacrificial rituals, all while harboring fears that robots might steal their jobs. This chaotic and rapid transformation is the epitome of compressed modernity—elements from different eras forced into a single point in time and space.

Compressed modernity (压缩现代性) describes the phenomenon where time and space are extremely condensed during social change. When modernization occurs too rapidly, pre-modern (e.g., traditional agrarian society), modern (e.g., industrial cities), and post-modern (e.g., digital risks and globalization) elements are forced to coexist, forming a fluid and composite system.

South Korea serves as a prime example: in the latter half of the 20th century, it achieved in just 50 years the industrialization and economic growth that took Western nations 200–300 years. This resulted in a society that simultaneously exhibits the high-tech prowess of a developed nation, the poverty issues of an underdeveloped one, and unique cultural conflicts. For instance, a young person in Seoul might pursue individualism (post-modern) while remaining shackled by traditional family obligations (pre-modern), all while facing economic instability (modern risk). This compression has birthed a "bali-bali" (hurry-up) culture—prioritizing results, metrics, and efficiency—but it also brings composite risks, such as environmental crises or deep social divisions.

Kyung-Sup Chang expanded this concept to East Asia, noting that China’s rapid transformation since the Reform and Opening-up is similar: traditional family values are interwoven with modern individualism—a shift analyzed by scholars like Yunxiang Yan. Essentially, compressed modernity reveals the price of rapid development: history is folded, and society moves forward through its own contradictions.

example_sentence.zh: 在巴西里约热内卢的贫民窟改造项目中，压缩现代性现象表现为原住民社区的传统手工艺与现代数字创业公司共存，居民们既参与古老节日庆典，又通过社交媒体推广业务，同时面临快速城市化带来的住房短缺问题。
example_sentence.en: In the favela redevelopment project in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, the phenomenon of compressed modernity manifests as the coexistence of traditional crafts from indigenous communities with modern digital startups, where residents engage in ancient festivals while promoting businesses via social media, all while confronting housing shortages driven by rapid urbanization.
